Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT A. Francisco Gold Condominium II EDSA Cor. Mapagmahal St., Diliman Quezon City LEGAL SERVICE RAMON SAN PASCUAL Executive Director, PLPCD DILG Legal Opinion No. II s. 2011 OCT 04 2011 2/F AVECCS Bldg., Kamias Road cor. K-J Street, East Kamias, Quezon City EDEN R. DIVINA GRACIA Executive Director, PNGOC JUNICE DEMETERIO MELGAR Secretary General, RHAN BENJAMIN D. DE LEON President, The Forum Gentlemen and Ladies: This has reference to your letter dated 06 April 2011 requesting this Department to conduct an investigation and to exert all its available powers to have the Protection of the Unborn Child Ordinance of 2011 of Barangay Ayala Alabang and similar ordinances enacted by other local government units (LGUs) stopped or amended to be compliant with national laws and for the Secretary of this Department to send a communication to all LGUs expressing the Department's position on these matters. At the outset, the we deemed it proper to discuss certain principles involving the power of the local sanggunians to enact ordinances. Under Section l, Article V [ of the 1987 Constitution, the legislative power shall be vested in the Congress of the Philippines which shall consist of a Senate and a House of Representatives, except to the extent reserved to the people by the provision on initiative and referendum. This legislative power was delegated by Congress to the local sanggunian by virtue of Section 48 of the Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160). While such power was validly delegated to local government units (LGUs), the exercise of such power by the delegated entities is absolute. In Magtajas vs. Pryce Properties and PAGCOR, G.R. No. 111097, 20 July 1994 the Supreme Court enumerated the following substantive requirements of a valid ordinance: I. It must not contravene the Constitution or any statute; 2. It must not be unfair or oppressive; 3. It must not be partial or discriminatory; 4. It must not prohibit but may regulate trade; 5. It must be general and consistent with public policy; and 6. It must not be unreasonable. Thus, the local legislative power delegated to an LGU is in reality not eminent but "inferior" since it must conform to the limits imposed by the delegating authority which is the Congress of the Philippines. The national legislature is still the principal of the LGUs and the latter cannot go against the statues passed by the principal.

2- In the meantime, pursuant to the power of general supervision of the President over all local government units, which was delegated to the DILG Secretary by virtue of Administrative Order No. 267 dated February 18, 1992, the Secretary of the DILG exercises general supervision over local government units. The power of supervision is defined as "the power ofa superior office to see to it that lower officers perform their functions in accordance with law" (Bito-Onon vs. Fernandez, et al., G.R. No. 139813, 31 January 2001). Supervising officers merely sees to it that the rules are followed, but he himself does not lay down such rules, nor does he have the discretion to modify or replace them. If the rules are not observed, he may order the work done or re-done to conform to the prescribed rules (supra). As general supervisor therefore of LGUs, it is incumbent for this Department to call upon all LGUs to abide by the pertinent laws. It may be recalled that the primary basis of Barangay Ayala Alabang in their Barangay Ordinance No. l, series of 2011 was Republic Act 5921 or the Pharmacy Law. In fact, in Section 7 of the said Barangay Ordinance, the Sangguniang Barangay of Ayala Alabang incorporated as an integral part thereof Section 37 of RA 5921 as follows: "Section 3Z Provisions relative to dispensing of anti- conceptional substances and devices. No drug or chemical product or device capable of provoking abortion or preventing conception as classified by the Food and Drug Administration shall be delivered or sold to any person without a proper prescription by a duly licensed physician. Let it be noted that the Board of Pharmacy and the Food and Drug Administration have already made their respective positions on the matter. The Board of Pharmacy maintained that RA 5921 or the Pharmacy Law was enacted mainly for the objective of supervision, control and regulation of the practice of pharmacy in the country and that the Board of Pharmacy is the only and exclusive body authorized to regulate and supervise pharmacists and impose penalties on them in case they were found guilty of violation of its provision. There is no provision in the Pharmacy Law that states that such power has been delegated or can be delegated to a different body or agency. The FDA also maintained that it is the proper agency that should classify whether a drug or chemical product or device is indeed capable of provoking abortion or preventing conception. On the part of this Department, considering that we are also tasked to interpret the provisions of the Local Government Code of 1991, the Department has already intimated as to the legal infirmity of the subject Ordinance for the following reasons: l. The subject Barangay Ordinance prescribes fines under Section 8 thereof in an amount not less than but not exceeding Php5,OOO.OO. Under Section 391 (a)(14) of the Local Government Code of 1991, the Sangguniang Barangay is authorized only to '(P)rescribe fines in amounts not exceeding One Thousand Pessos (Phpl,000.00) for violation of barangay Ordinances. " 2. The subject Barangay Ordinance imposed the penalty of imprisonment under Section 8.

-3- May we note that the Sangguniang Barangay has no authority to impose a penalty of imprisonment in cases of violation of barangay ordinances. Only the Sangguniang Panlungsod/Bayan/Panlalawigan are authorized to do so. As to the Ordinances recently passed by the 7 barangays of Balanga City in Bataan, which were averred to have violated other laws such as RA 7394 (Consumer Act of the Philippines), RAA 3721 (Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act), RA 9711 (Food and Drug Administration Act of 2009) and RA 9710 (Magna Carta of Women), we are of the view that there is a need to seek first the position of the government agencies tasked to implement the aforesaid laws. Besides, the Department is not aware on whether said Ordinances passed by the 7 barangays of Balanga City are still subject to the review power of the Sangguniang Panlungsod of Balanga City. Because if they are, then Section 57 (c) of the Local Government Code of 1991 is applicable, that is, the Sangguniang Panlungsod shall return the barangay ordinance with its comments and recommendations to the sangguniang barangay concerned for adjustment, amendment, or modification; in which case, ghg effectivity of the barangay ordinance is suspended until such time as the revision called for is effected. Assuming that the aforesaid Ordinances of the 7 barangays of Balanga City have already passed the review of the Sangguniang Panlungsod, then the only remedy is the filing of an action for Declaratory Relief under Section l, Rule 63 of the Rules of Court, thus: Section I. Who may file petition. — Any person interested under a deed, will, contract or other written instrument, whose rights are affected by a statute, executive order or regulation, ordinance, or any other governmental regulation may, before breach or violation thereof; bring an action in the appropriate Regional Trial Court to determine any question of construction or validity arising, and for a declaration of his rights or duties, thereunder. In view of the foregoing, please be informed that this Department shall exert all its available efforts advising all LGUs to abide by the pertinent laws. We hope to have addressed your concern accordingly. Very truly yours, . JESU B. QUEIV Director III Ls/17 HON. ENRIQUE T. ONA Secretary Department of Health San Lazaro Compound, Sta. Cruz Manila
